passage: Early on Gudi Padwa morning, Mahima Tai swept the yard in front of the village house and handed five-year-old Tushar a small bowl of orange colour. 'Your job: fill every petal on this side.' Tushar crouched, tongue between his teeth, and pinched the colour out slowly. Some fell outside the lines. Mahima Tai didn't fix it. When the neighbours came to look, Tushar stood by his side of the rangoli with orange fingers and announced, 'I made this part.' That night he asked, 'When's the next festival?'

qa.q: What did Mahima Tai hand Tushar?
qa.a: A small bowl of orange colour.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he announced, 'I made this part'?
qa.a: He felt proud and important, having done a real job for the festival.

qa.q: What did Mahima Tai get right in giving Tushar the task?
qa.a: She gave him a clear, real job and didn't fix his mistakes, so that part of the rangoli truly felt like his.

qa.q: How might Mahima Tai feel hearing Tushar ask, 'When's the next festival?'
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and amused, seeing that he now looks forward to festivals.

grounding: Shows a young child given a real part in making a festival rangoli, who is proud of the task and starts looking forward to the next festival.

passage: The week before Lunar New Year, Mr. Chen from the bakery downstairs asked five-year-old Beatriz if she could help. 'Very important job. These lanterns go on the low hooks.' Beatriz stood on a stool, Mamãe holding her waist, and hung six red lanterns one by one, counting in Portuguese. One hung crooked. Mr. Chen left it. All week Beatriz pointed out 'my lanterns' to every customer, and she circled the date on the kitchen calendar with a red crayon.

qa.q: How many lanterns did Beatriz hang?
qa.a: Six red lanterns.

qa.q: How did Beatriz feel about 'my lanterns' all week?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited, showing them to every customer as her own work.

qa.q: What made Mr. Chen's invitation meaningful for Beatriz?
qa.a: He called it an important job, gave her a real task at her height and left the crooked lantern, so it truly felt like hers.

qa.q: How might Mr. Chen's customers feel when Beatriz shows off her lanterns?
qa.a: They would likely feel charmed and drawn into the festival mood by her pride.

grounding: Illustrates a young child proud to be given a real task in preparing for a festival, which gives her a place in the community and a date to look forward to.

passage:
On Makar Sankranti the whole terrace was full of kites, but the wind kept dying.

Pankaj bhaiya from next door handed Salma, five, the spool. "Hold tight. When I say, let it go slowly. You're in charge of the string."

Salma gripped the wooden spool with both hands. Twice the kite flopped down. Twice Pankaj ran it up again.

Then a gust came. "Now, Salma!" She let the string unroll, round and round, and the red kite climbed higher than the water tank.

"You did it!" Pankaj shouted.

Salma didn't let go of the spool until dinner. That night she asked Ammi how many sleeps until the next Sankranti.

qa.q: How high did the red kite climb?
qa.a: The red kite climbed higher than the water tank.

qa.q: How did Salma feel when the kite climbed so high?
qa.a: Salma felt proud and thrilled, holding on to the spool until dinner.

qa.q: Why was giving Salma the spool a good idea?
qa.a: A real job made her part of the festival, not just a watcher, and now she is counting the sleeps until the next one.

qa.q: What was it like for Pankaj when the kite finally rose?
qa.a: Pankaj was excited and happy for Salma, shouting 'You did it!'

grounding: Shows a young child given a real task at a kite festival despite a dying wind, proud to belong and already looking forward to the next one.

passage:
The night before Diwali, Ira drew the rangoli outline in white chalk outside the flat door in Andheri. "Disha, you fill the petals. Pink only, inside the lines."

Disha, four, knelt with the pink powder in her fist. Most of it went inside the lines. Some went on her socks.

The neighbour aunty stopped on the stairs. "Who made these lovely petals?"

"Me!" Disha jumped up, pink to the elbows. "Ira didi did the lines. I did the colour."

She wouldn't let anyone step near the rangoli all evening, and at bedtime she asked how many days till Holi, when there would be even more colours.

qa.q: What colour did Disha fill the petals with?
qa.a: Disha filled the petals with pink.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when the neighbour aunty praised the petals?
qa.a: Disha felt proud and delighted, jumping up to claim her part.

qa.q: How could Ira keep Disha involved in festivals?
qa.a: Keep giving her a real part, like filling colours, with simple rules she can manage.

qa.q: How might Ira see Disha's messy help?
qa.a: Ira likely finds it sweet and is happy to share the credit, since she planned a job just for Disha.

grounding: Shows a young child proud of a real task in making a Diwali rangoli, feeling part of the festival and looking forward to the next.

passage:
"Can I make one?" Dolma asked, standing on a stool in the kitchen.
"Losar khapse need small hands," said Amala, giving her a strip of dough. "Twist it like this, then pinch the ends."
Dolma twisted. The dough broke. "Oh no."
"Try again. Softer."
The second one held. "Amala, look! A real one!"
"A real one," Amala agreed, placing it on the tray with the others.
When her friend Sabina came over, Dolma dragged her straight to the tray. "That one's mine. The twisty one."
"Can I make one too?"
Amala nodded. Dolma handed Sabina a strip of dough, very seriously. "Softer. Like this."

qa.q: What did Amala give Dolma?
qa.a: Amala gave her a strip of dough.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when the second khapse held?
qa.a: Dolma felt proud and excited, calling out that she had made a real one.

qa.q: What made Dolma's part in Losar meaningful?
qa.a: Amala gave her a real task, let her try again after a mistake, and put her khapse on the tray with the others.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel when Dolma teaches her?
qa.a: Sabina probably feels welcomed and excited to join in a festival that isn't her own.

grounding: Shows a young child proud of a real festival task and eager to share her place in it with a friend.

passage:
Preschool note, Diwali week.
Today the children made a rangoli at the entrance. I gave Yogesh the yellow powder and the job of filling the petals. He took it very seriously, tongue out, pinching the colour just as I showed him. When Harish stepped on a corner, Yogesh cried "Careful!" and fixed it himself. At home time he dragged his father to see it. "I made the yellow!" He asked me three times if we will make one again next year.

qa.q: What colour did Yogesh fill the petals with?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel showing the rangoli to his father?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited, dragging his father to see it and announcing that he made the yellow.

qa.q: Why was giving Yogesh a real task a good idea?
qa.a: A real job made him feel part of the festival and the group, and gave him something to look forward to next year.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when Yogesh shouted "Careful!"?
qa.a: Harish may have felt a bit startled or embarrassed at stepping on the corner.

grounding: It illustrates a child proud to have a real task in making a festival rangoli, giving him a place in the group.
